summary: Introduces two technology-independent extensions to GMPLS. One defines a Data Channel Switching Capable switching type for interfaces that switch a whole digital channel. The other defines a new label type that lets a set of channels be described together.

plainLanguage.summary: GMPLS sets up labelled paths across a network. This RFC adds two things to it: a way to describe an interface that carries one whole channel, and a way to send several labels in the same path, each with its own list of subchannels.

questions: what is the generalized channel_set label
what is data channel switching capable
what is switching type 125 in gmpls
subtitle: Two additions to GMPLS: switching a whole channel, and carrying several labels in one path.

tldr.problem: GMPLS had no switching type for a link that carries one whole digital channel, and no way to send several data plane labels in a single path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Data Channel Switching Capable switching type with the value 125, and a Generalized Channel_Set label object that carries a list of subchannels, each with its own label.
tldr.outcome: A GMPLS path can be set up over a single-channel interface and can carry a set of labels together, which is what Ethernet services with many VLAN identifiers need.

facts.label: Subobject size
facts.value: A multiple of 4 bytes, at least 4

today: RFC 6002 is a Proposed Standard. It updates the GMPLS signalling and switching type definitions of RFC 3471, RFC 3473, RFC 3945, RFC 4202, RFC 4203 and RFC 5307, and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Two Extensions
sections.content:
The document describes two technology-independent extensions to Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching. Both were initially defined in the context of Ethernet services, in RFC 6004 and RFC 6005, but they are generic in nature and may be useful to any switching technology controlled through GMPLS.

The first extension defines a new switching type called Data Channel Switching Capable, or DCSC. DCSC interfaces are able to support switching of the whole digital channel presented on single-channel interfaces. The second extension defines a new type of generalized label and updates the related objects. The new label is called the Generalized Channel_Set Label and allows more than one data plane label to be controlled as part of one GMPLS label switched path.
sections.plainLanguage: The first addition names a kind of interface that carries one channel and switches it whole. The second addition lets one path hold several labels at once, instead of one label per path.

sections.title: Where DCSC Fits Among the Switching Types
sections.content:
The current GMPLS switching types are defined in RFC 3945 and RFC 3471, and support switching at the packet, frame, time-slot, frequency and fiber granularities. Parallel definitions are also made in RFC 4202, RFC 4203 and RFC 5307.

One type of switching is not well represented in that set: switching where all the data received on an ingress port is switched through the network to an egress port. There are similarities with the opaque single wavelength case of Section 3.5 of RFC 4202, but this port-to-port switching is not limited to the optical technology implied by the frequency switching type. Fiber switching is similar too, but it is restricted to fiber ports and also supports multiple data channels within a fiber port.

The new switching type is called Data Channel Switching Capable. Port switching would be a more intuitive name, but it collides with packet switching, so it is not used. DCSC interfaces support switching of the whole digital channel presented on single-channel interfaces. Interfaces that inherently support multiple channels, such as wavelength division multiplexing and channelised TDM interfaces, are specifically excluded from this type. Any interface that can be represented as a single digital channel is included. The examples given are concatenated TDM and line-encoded interfaces. Framed interfaces may also be included when they support switching at interface granularity, for example Ethernet terminated at the physical port level, where all the traffic received on a port is switched to a physical port at the path egress.

DCSC is represented in GMPLS using the value 125. That value is carried in the routing protocols in the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor of RFC 4202, and used in OSPF and IS-IS. Those documents are not otherwise modified.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS already has switching types for packets, frames, time slots, wavelengths and whole fibres. The new type covers the case of an interface that carries one channel: everything that arrives on it is switched to another port. Interfaces that carry several channels are excluded, because they are a different case.

sections.title: Using the New Switching Type
sections.content:
The DCSC switching type may be used with the Generalized Label Request object of RFC 3473, or with the Generalized Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST object defined in the document. Port labels, as defined in RFC 3471, should be used for paths signalled with the DCSC switching type.

Nodes that do not support the DCSC switching type and receive a Path message with a label request containing it behave in the way nodes generally handle an unsupported switching type: per RFC 3473, they generate a PathErr message with a Routing problem, Unsupported Encoding indication. An ingress node that initiated such a Path message, on receiving that error, notifies the requesting application user as appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that does not know the new switching type rejects the request with the usual error for an unknown encoding, and the node that asked tells the application which asked for the path.

sections.title: Why a Label Can Hold Several Labels
sections.content:
The document defines a new type of generalized label and updates the related objects, updating the label-related definitions of RFC 3473. The ability to communicate more than one label as part of the same path was motivated by the support for communicating one or more VLAN identifiers. Simply concatenating labels, as done in RFC 4606, was deemed impractical given the large number of VLAN identifiers, up to 4096, that may need to be communicated. The formats defined here are not technology specific and may be useful for other switching technologies, and the LABEL_SET object of RFC 3473 serves as the foundation for them.

The Generalized Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST object indicates that the Generalized Channel_Set LABEL object is to be used with the associated path. Its format is the same as the Generalized LABEL_REQUEST object and uses a C-Type of 5.

The Generalized Channel_Set LABEL object communicates one or more labels, all of which can be used equivalently in the data path associated with a single path. Its format is based on the LABEL_SET object of RFC 3473, and differs from it in that the full set may be represented in a single object rather than the multiple objects that the LABEL_SET object requires. The object must be used on paths that use the Generalized Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST object, and it must be processed per RFC 3473. Make-before-break procedures should be used when modifying the Channel_Set LABEL object.
sections.plainLanguage: One path can carry several labels, and each of them works the same way in the data path. The reason is that a service may need a list of VLAN identifiers, and there can be thousands of them, so sending one label per identifier as separate objects does not scale.

sections.title: The Format of the Channel Set Label
sections.content:
The Generalized Channel_Set LABEL object has Class 16 and C-Type 4, and its body is a list of Channel_Set Subobjects, one after another.

The size of a Channel_Set Subobject is measured in bytes and must always be a multiple of 4, and at least 4. Its first three fields are the Action, 8 bits, which is defined in RFC 3471, with range actions recommended where possible to keep the object small; the Number of Subchannels, 10 bits, which says how many subchannels the subobject carries; and the Label Type, 14 bits, described in RFC 3473. The subchannels follow, each of variable length and described in RFC 3471, and the subchannel field might not be 32-bit aligned. Padding is used to make the length of the subobject a multiple of 4 bytes, and it is only required when the subchannels do not come out aligned.

When the number of subchannels needed exceeds the limit of the field, which is 1024, several Channel_Set Subobjects must be used. The size of the subobject may result in a Path message being larger than a single unfragmented IP packet. The document notes that a value of zero in the number of subchannels has a special meaning and may be used in either the LABEL or the UPSTREAM_LABEL object: it indicates that the subchannels used in the corresponding direction must match the subchannels carried in the reverse direction's label object. When zero is used, no subchannels are included in the subobject and only one Channel_Set Subobject may be present, and the zero value must not be used in both the LABEL and the UPSTREAM_LABEL objects of the same path. Label values that are unacceptable continue to be handled as RFC 3209 and RFC 3473 require, with a PathErr or ResvErr message carrying a Routing problem, Unacceptable label value indication. So a Resv message with a zero in both the LABEL and the UPSTREAM_LABEL objects makes the node generate a ResvErr.

The padding field must be included when the bits represented by all the subchannel fields do not leave the subobject 32-bit aligned, and when present its length must make the subobject aligned. It must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, and those bits should be passed through unmodified by transit nodes. The overall length of a subobject is determined by the number of subchannels, the size of each subchannel field, and any required padding, and the size of the subchannel field is uniquely identified by the Label Type field.
sections.plainLanguage: The object is a list of subobjects, each holding a count, a label type and the labels themselves. The list is padded so that it fits the alignment rules. A count of zero is a special case meaning that the two directions of the path use the same subchannels.

sections.title: The Other Label Objects and Older Nodes
sections.content:
Because the document introduces a new LABEL object, the formats of the other label-related objects and subobjects are also affected, although their processing is not modified and remains as their respective specifications state. The other label-related objects and subobjects are defined in RFC 3473 and are the SUGGESTED_LABEL object, the LABEL_SET object, the ACCEPTABLE_LABEL_SET object, the UPSTREAM_LABEL object, the RECOVERY_LABEL object, the Label ERO subobject and the Label RRO subobject.

Each of them contains a Label field, and all of those may carry any label type. Since any label type may be carried, the introduction of a new label type means that it may be carried in the Label field of each of these objects and subobjects, and no new definition needs to be given, because their original specification is label-type agnostic.

Nodes that do not support the Generalized Channel_Set Label formats first receive a Path message containing the Generalized Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST object. Such a node, per RFC 3209, answers with a PathErr carrying the error code Unknown object C_Type. An ingress node that initiated such a Path message, on receiving that error, notifies the requesting application user as appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The other places where a label can appear, such as the recorded route and the upstream label, can all carry the new label type without any change to their own definitions. A node that does not know the new request object refuses it with an unknown-object error.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA has made three assignments. In the Switching Types section of the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry, the value 125 has been assigned to Data Channel Switching Capable, and the assignment is reflected in the IANAGmplsSwitchingTypeTC object of the IANA-GMPLS-TC-MIB. In the Class Names, Class Numbers and Class Types section of the RSVP PARAMETERS registry, a new class type has been added for the existing LABEL_REQUEST object class number 19, with the value 5 for Generalized Channel_Set. A new class type has also been added for the existing RSVP_LABEL object class number 16, with the value 4 for Generalized Channel_Set.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA for three numbers: one for the new switching type, one for the new request object and one for the new label object.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces new message object formats for use in GMPLS signalling. It does not introduce any new signalling messages, nor change the relationship between label switching routers that are adjacent in the control plane, and so it introduces no additional security considerations. The security considerations of RFC 3473 apply, and the existing framework for MPLS and GMPLS security is documented in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes how routers talk to each other or what is protected between them, so the existing security rules for GMPLS signalling apply unchanged.

fields.name: Action
fields.desc: The action defined in RFC 3471. Range actions keep the object small.

fields.name: Num Subchannels
fields.desc: How many subchannels this subobject carries. A value of zero has a special meaning.

fields.name: Label Type
fields.desc: The type of the labels that follow, which also fixes their size.

viz.caption: THE THREE OBJECTS THE DOCUMENT ADDS OR CHANGES

cells: Describes an interface that carries and switches one whole digital channel
Asks for the Generalized Channel_Set LABEL object on the path
Carries the list of subchannels, each with its own label

viz.caption: THE RULES THE SUBOBJECT HAS TO FOLLOW

items.title: Size
items.text: A multiple of 4 bytes, and at least 4 bytes.

items.title: Subchannel limit
items.text: At most 1024 subchannels in one subobject; more needs several subobjects.

items.title: A count of zero
items.text: Means the two directions use the same subchannels. Only one subobject may then be present.

items.title: Padding
items.text: Fills the subobject to a 32-bit boundary, set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.
